# True or false: Architecture

Microservices, rewrites, decision records, APIs and debt. Test your instincts on the decisions that are expensive to reverse.

11 statements (Foundation 2, Standard 9). Decide whether each one is true or false before you open the answer. Every answer says why and links to the page that teaches it.

Prefer the terminal? From the repository root, run `python3 exercises/quiz.py --area architecture`.

### 1. Splitting a slow system into microservices is usually the first fix for performance problems.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Scale in order: measure, fix the slow query or code path, add caching, move work to queues, scale out, and only then partition data or split services. Each step is cheaper and less risky than the next. Most systems never need the last two, and a modular monolith serves many organisations better.

Read more: [playbook/architecture/scaling.md](../../playbook/architecture/scaling.md)

</details>

### 2. Services that must always be deployed together are a sign of a distributed monolith.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** If services cannot change on their own, you pay the network and operations cost of services without their independence. Either merge them back or fix the boundaries between them. A monolith with clear modules is better than this.

Read more: [playbook/architecture/scaling.md](../../playbook/architecture/scaling.md)

</details>

### 3. When a core system is 20 years old, a full rewrite with a single go-live date is usually the safest path.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Big-bang rewrites tend to run late, chase a moving target and arrive missing features nobody wrote down. Replace the old system piece by piece behind a stable interface, using the strangler fig pattern. Each slice ships value, so the programme can stop at any point and still have paid for itself.

Read more: [playbook/architecture/legacy-modernisation.md](../../playbook/architecture/legacy-modernisation.md)

</details>

### 4. When the built system differs from an accepted ADR, you should edit the ADR to match what was built.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Editing the record erases the history of why the plan changed. Write a new ADR that supersedes the old one. The gap between the plan and reality is useful information for whoever comes next.

Read more: [playbook/architecture/decision-records.md](../../playbook/architecture/decision-records.md)

</details>

### 5. Paying down technical debt from a fixed share of every cycle usually works better than waiting for a dedicated refactoring quarter.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** Refactoring quarters are hard to fund and rarely arrive. Pay debt down continuously from a fixed share of every team's capacity. Rank the register each quarter by the cost each item causes today.

Read more: [playbook/architecture/technical-debt.md](../../playbook/architecture/technical-debt.md)

</details>

### 6. Technical debt is easier to fund when it is described by the cost it causes today.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** 'The code is ugly' does not compete with a feature for budget. Price the interest in time lost, failures, risk or missed opportunity. Debt you can name, price and rank becomes a normal business decision.

Read more: [playbook/architecture/technical-debt.md](../../playbook/architecture/technical-debt.md)

</details>

### 7. Adding user ID as a metric label is a good way to debug problems for individual users.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Each distinct label value creates a new time series, so user IDs make metric cardinality and cost explode. Put user IDs in traces and logs instead. Enforce this with a rule in the OpenTelemetry Collector.

Read more: [playbook/architecture/observability.md](../../playbook/architecture/observability.md)

</details>

### 8. Returning HTTP 200 with an error message in the body is a fine way to report API errors.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Clients, proxies and monitoring read the status code, so a 200 hides the failure from all of them. Use real status codes and the Problem Details format (RFC 9457). One error shape across the organisation means consumers learn it once.

Read more: [playbook/architecture/api-standards.md](../../playbook/architecture/api-standards.md)

</details>

### 9. Unsafe POST requests, such as payments, should accept an Idempotency-Key so that retries do not create duplicates.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** Networks fail after a request is processed but before the reply arrives, so clients retry. Without an idempotency key, a retry can charge a customer twice. Test the retry path, not only the happy path.

Read more: [playbook/architecture/api-standards.md](../../playbook/architecture/api-standards.md)

</details>

### 10. You can copy the rings from a well-known external tech radar, because what works elsewhere will work for you.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** External radars show what works in other organisations. Your rings depend on your own skills, scale and hosting. An Adopt entry must also be something your platform team can support on the golden path.

Read more: [playbook/architecture/tech-radar.md](../../playbook/architecture/tech-radar.md)

</details>

### 11. An RFC can be decided by one named approver even when some commenters still disagree.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** Waiting for full agreement leads to comment periods that never end and design by committee. Each RFC has a fixed time box and one named approver who decides with the information available. Consensus is welcome, not required.

Read more: [playbook/architecture/rfcs.md](../../playbook/architecture/rfcs.md)

</details>
